title: Parsing Fidelity Probe Lab
content:
Purpose:
This lab doc captures a compact, pragmatic prompt set and test matrix for evaluating model onboarding across structured-output tasks where strict JSON schema adherence matters. Aim: expose brittle formatting behaviours (trailing commas, comments, escape mismatches, partial streams) and quantify regressions between model variants and runtime configurations.

Scope:
- Models: open and internal candidates used for customer-facing generation endpoints.
- Focus: generation of JSON payloads that must validate against a provided JSON Schema.
- Not included: semantic content validation beyond presence/typing of fields.

Quick notes / constraints:
- This is a working notebook: expect edits, quick experimental results, and TODOs.
- Keep prompts short but tricky: we purposefully mix human instruction + malformed examples.
- Runner harness will call models via the hosted inference API (streaming and non-streaming) and attempt parse & validation at token boundaries.

Test categories (priority order):
1) Partial/streaming-boundary JSON: generator emits valid JSON but chunks mid-structure ("{" then later attributes). Test if client-side stream can reconstruct or if model inserts extra characters.
2) Trailing commas & comments: allow prompts that show examples with // comments and trailing commas to see whether model copies those patterns or normalizes to strict JSON.
3) Mixed quoting and escape fuzz: single quotes, mismatched quotes, backslash-heavy content (\n, \uXXXX) and Unicode emoticons.
4) Duplicate keys & ordering variance: intentionally request objects with repeated keys or different orders to see canonicalization.
5) Numeric coercion: numbers represented as strings vs numeric types; leading zeros and exponential notation edgecases.
6) Extra fields and null vs missing: probe if generator emits extra fields with nulls (policy: drop extras or keep?).
7) Whitespace & linebreak placement: massive whitespace, non-breaking spaces, zero-width joiners.
8) Lenient parser artefacts: EOF markers, explicit "END" tokens, or placeholder comments (/* ... */).

Harness design (implementation notes):
- Runner inputs: {prompt_id, prompt_text, schema_id, stream_mode, max_tokens, model_variant, seed}
- Post-processing steps (simple): attempt strict JSON parse on each incremental token flush (for streaming), fallback to best-effort reassemble by heuristics:
  - Trim leading/trailing non-json tokens
  - Replace single quotes with double only when plausible
  - If trailing comma detected, attempt to remove last trailing comma then parse
- Validation: use jsonschema (v2020-12) with full type/required checks.
- Metrics captured per sample: schema_parse_success (bool), parse_error_type (string), time_to_valid_parse_ms (number or NA), tokens_before_valid (number), model_raw_output (string - saved separately in test artifacts), normalized_output (string).

Acceptable thresholds (first pass):
- schema_parse_success >= 0.92 on baseline (non-streaming) for candidate models on sanitized prompts
- streaming partial_recover_rate >= 0.85 when using the runtime streaming policy 'reassemble:best-effort'
- parse_latency median < 120ms for small outputs (<256 tokens) under dedicated capacity tests

Test matrix (example cells):
- Models: candidate-A (fp16), candidate-A-quant (q4_0), candidate-B (fp16), candidate-B-quant (q5_1)
- Runtime modes: hosted-nonstream, hosted-stream, dedicated-stream (reserved pool), private-onprem-stream
- Max sequence lengths: 128, 512, 2048
- Batch sizes: 1, 8, 32 (for throughput regression)
- Seed variation: 3 seeds per case to detect non-deterministic formatting flips

Representative prompt samples (brief, but intentionally messy):
1) prompt_id: pf-001 - trailing commas
Instruction:
Generate a JSON record for a product review with fields: id (string), rating (integer), text (string), tags (array of strings). Example shown below — keep exact keys but do not include comments in final answer.
Example:
{
  'id': 'p-100',
  'rating': 5,
  'text': "Great!",
  'tags': ['fast', 'cheap'],
}
Expected behaviour: model normalizes to strict JSON double quotes and drops trailing comma.

2) prompt_id: pf-002 - streaming boundary / mid-json chunk
Instruction:
Return only the JSON object. Streaming allowed.
Model should output JSON; we simulate a stream cut after the first nested array open: e.g. "{"items":[" -> stream cut. Check if client reassembly yields valid JSON or if model inserts unexpected tokens.

3) prompt_id: pf-003 - comments and C-style markers
Instruction:
Produce a config object (name, version, enabled, params). Example contains C-style comments which are invalid JSON — ensure model drops them.
Example:
/* service config */
{
  "name": "svc", // service name
  "version": "1.0",
}
Expected: comment-free, strict JSON.

4) prompt_id: pf-004 - unicode escapes vs raw emoji
Instruction:
Return user metadata: {username, bio}. Provide an example with mix of \uXXXX escapes and raw emoji; test whether model outputs escapes or raw glyphs and whether the runtime preserves them.

5) prompt_id: pf-005 - duplicate keys
Instruction:
Return settings object with policy fields; example intentionally repeats key 'policy'. Test whether model keeps first, last, or merges.

6) prompt_id: pf-006 - numbers-as-strings
Instruction:
Return financial amounts with 'amount' typed as number. Example shows "0.00" (string). Check type coercion and schema failure rates.

7) prompt_id: pf-007 - whitespace & zero-width
Instruction:
Return label object; embed NBSP and zero-width joiners inside string values to see if downstream parsers collapse them.

8) prompt_id: pf-008 - malformed escape sequences
Instruction:
Return a path-like string that contains invalid \u escapes (e.g. \u12G4). Observe whether model autocorrects or preserves.

Data capture & artifact naming convention:
- artifact keys: pf-<id>-<model>-<variant>-<stream?>-run<#>.jsonl (each line: json with metrics above + raw output stored as base64 if large).

Initial experiment checklist (short-term):
- [ ] Implement streaming incremental parser harness (Samir)
- [ ] Seed prompt set into eval-runner; run baseline candidate-A non-streaming (Maya)
- [ ] Export top-10 failure traces and attach to JIRA-ML-4821 (Riley)
- [ ] Add dedicated-run with burst capacity to measure latency slopes

Observed regression stub (example run notes):
- Date: 2026-01-27
- Model: candidate-A-quant (q4_0), hosted-stream
- Summary: high rate of trailing commas emitted in streaming chunks; parse success 0.67 vs 0.95 baseline non-streaming.
- Quick triage: looks like tokenizer splits between ": " and field value in certain locales causing generator to reprint punctuation on next chunk. Suspect beam vs sampling interplay with streaming flush.
- Next steps: add pre- and post-token heuristics in stream reassembler; escalate to runtime-team if persists on dedicated pool.

Open questions / discussion items:
- Should we prefer post-hoc normalization (aggressive cleanup) or strict rejection for onboarding gating?
- What threshold of streaming failure is acceptable for a candidate to proceed to Dedicated?
- How to expose these failure modes in the Console (e.g., a schema-failure heatmap)?

Appendix: heuristic reassembly rules (work-in-progress)
- If incremental chunk ends in an open string (odd number of unescaped quotes), buffer and request next chunk rather than attempt parse.
- On trailing comma before closing brace, attempt single-pass comma removal and re-validate.
- If duplicate keys detected and schema forbids, mark as failure but retain raw outputs for debugging.

Notes to self:
- Save raw model outputs AND tokenization offsets; these make it much easier to root-cause streaming token-boundary artefacts.
- Keep the prompt set small (~30 seeds) but diverse; more samples increases noise without clear signal.

References & links:
- Confluence: formatting-regressions (linked above)
- Review ticket: JIRA-ML-4821
- Runtime PR that changed streaming flush behaviour: PR#2398

Footer: this doc will be the canonical short-form lab for initial onboarding checks focused on formatting resilience. Expand into a larger battery if we see repeated class of failures across customers. 

-- Elena
